title: Nur al-Din Ali and the Damsel Anis Al-Jalis

keywords: nur al-din ali and the damsel anis al-jalis
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived a wise vizier named Al-Fazl, who served King Muhammad bin Sulayman. The king had commissioned him to purchase a maiden of supreme beauty, intelligence, and musical talent. The vizier found such a maiden, named Anis al-Jalis, who had mastered calligraphy, grammar, history, and the playing of the lute.

Before presenting her to the king, the vizier brought her to his own palace to rest. There, his noble son, Nur al-Din Ali, beheld her, and the two young people fell deeply in love. Realizing that true affection cannot be commanded by royal decree, the vizier permitted them to wed, but warned his son to live with modest prudence.

When the elder vizier passed away, a jealous rival vizier, Al-Muin, reported to the king that Nur al-Din had kept the royal maiden for himself. Faced with royal displeasure, Nur al-Din and Anis al-Jalis fled Basra by night, boarding a riverboat that carried them to the golden city of Baghdad.

Penniless in the great capital, they sought shelter in an enchanted pleasure garden on the banks of the Tigris. The keeper of the garden, an aged shaykh named Ibrahim, was so charmed by the young couple's modesty and Anis al-Jalis’s sublime lute playing that he brought them fruit, sweetmeats, and illuminated the garden pavilions with hundreds of colored candles.

The Caliph Harun al-Rashid, cruising the river in his royal barge, saw the brilliant illumination and sailed to the terrace in disguise. Listening from behind the rose trellises, the Caliph was enraptured by the maiden’s singing and Nur al-Din’s poetic wit. Revealing his identity, the Caliph did not punish them; instead, he admired their unwavering fidelity, granted them a royal pardon, and dispatched a royal decree to the King of Basra appointing Nur al-Din as governor in his father’s place.
moral: Sincere devotion, eloquence, and artistic excellence win the favor of monarchs and conquer all obstacles.
